Archaeological evidence indicates human habitation near the confluence of the ___E:Arkansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_River)___ and ___E:Little Arkansas Rivers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Arkansas_River)___ , the site of present-day Wichita, as early as 3000 BC.  In 1541, a ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Spain)___ expedition led by explorer ___E:Francisco Vázquez de Coronado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_V%C3%A1zquez_de_Coronado)___ found the area populated by the ___E:Quivira, or Wichita, people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_people)___ .

Prior to ___E:European settlement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_settlement_of_North_America)___ of the region, the site was in the territory of the ___E:Kiowa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiowa_people)___ .

Claimed first by ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France)___ as part of ___E:Louisiana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_(New_France))___ and later acquired by the United States with the ___E:Louisiana Purchase U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase)___ in 1803, it became part of ___E:Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ in 1854 and then the state of Kansas in 1861.

During this period, trader ___E:Jesse Chisholm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Chisholm)___ established a trading post at the site, one of several along a trail extending south to ___E:Texas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas)___ which became known as the ___E:Chisholm Trail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chisholm_Trail)___ .

In 1868, trader ___E:James R. Mead U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Mead_(pioneer))___ was among a group of investors who established a town company, and surveyor Darius Munger built a log structure for the company to serve as a hotel, community center, and post office.

Wichita's position on the Chisholm Trail made it a destination for ___E:cattle drives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_drive)___ traveling north from Texas to access railroads, which led to markets in eastern U.S. cities.

The ___E:Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atchison,_Topeka_and_Santa_Fe_Railway)___ reached the city in 1872.  As a result, Wichita became a railhead for the cattle drives, earning it the nickname "Cowtown".

Across the Arkansas River, the town of ___E:Delano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delano,_Wichita,_Kansas)___ became an entertainment destination for cattlemen thanks to its saloons, brothels, and lack of law enforcement.

Local arrest records show that Nellie, and Earp's common-law wife Sally, managed a brothel there from early 1874 to the middle of 1876.  The area had a reputation for violence until Wyatt officially joined the Wichita marshal's office on April 21, 1875, making $100 per month.

By the middle of the decade, the cattle trade had moved west to ___E:Dodge City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodge_City,_Kansas)___ .

Rapid immigration resulted in a ___E:speculative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speculation)___ land boom in the late 1880s, stimulating further expansion of the city. Fairmount College, which eventually grew into ___E:Wichita State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_State_University)___ , opened in 1886; Garfield University, which eventually became ___E:Friends University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends_University)___ , opened in 1887. In 1914 and 1915, deposits of ___E:oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum)___ and ___E:natural gas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas)___ were discovered in nearby ___E:Butler County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Kansas)___ .

Libraries were a priority for the early settlers of Wichita.

In 1873, the Wichita Library Association was granted with the “purpose of establishing and maintaining a public library and reading room and for the diffusion of knowledge and the promotion of intellectual improvement in the city of Wichita, Sedgwick county, Kansas."  Despite a plan set forth, this library and the following attempt at establishing one in 1874 never came to pass. Shortly later, another library association was formed by the same name of Wichita Library Association with a required membership fee of three dollars.
Women in the community organized events to raise funds.
However, this library struggled as well and stopped functioning in 1885. It wasn’t until the city hall was built that the development of a library began to take shape.

“In making their plans for housing the books, the board, then located in the Sedgwick block, petitioned and obtained permission from the city council to occupy rooms on the first floor of the city hall,"  and so it was this decision that proved successful in paving the way for future libraries in Wichita.
It was at this time that philanthropist, Andrew Carnegie, was providing funds for libraries in many states to be built.
In fact, Andrew Carnegie funded fifty-eight libraries in Kansas.
So, it is not surprising that in 1911, the city clerk wrote Andrew Carnegie for donations for a public library, which led to an offer of $75,000 for a building.

The Wichita Carnegie Library building opened to the public on May 14, 1915, and under the administration of Mr. Julius Lucht "the library was organized into its present departmental state, with a greatly augmented budget, staff and book collection."  The Wichita Carnegie Library was the main library for the city until 1967.

The city lies on the Arkansas River near the western edge of the ___E:Flint Hills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_Hills)___ in the Wellington-McPherson Lowlands region of the ___E:Great Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plains)___ .

The area's topography is characterized by the broad ___E:alluvial plain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alluvial_plain)___ of the Arkansas River valley and the moderately rolling slopes that rise to the higher lands on either side.
The Arkansas follows a winding course, south-southeast through Wichita, roughly bisecting the city. It is joined along its course by several tributaries, all of which flow generally south.
The largest is the Little Arkansas River, which enters the city from the north and joins the Arkansas immediately west of downtown.
Further east lies ___E:Chisholm Creek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chisholm_Creek)___ , which joins the Arkansas in the far southern part of the city.

The Gypsum is fed by its own tributary, Dry Creek.
Two more of the Arkansas's tributaries lie west of its course.
From east to west, these are Big Slough Creek and Cowskin Creek.

Both run south through the western part of the city. Fourmile Creek, a tributary of the ___E:Walnut River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walnut_River_(Kansas))___ , flows south through the far eastern part of the city.

Wichita lies within the ___E:humid subtropical climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate)___ zone ( ___E:Köppen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification)___ ___E:Cfa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate#Breakdown_of_letters)___ ), typically experiencing hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters.

Located on the ___E:Great Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plains)___ , far from any large moderating influences such as mountains or large bodies of water, Wichita often experiences severe weather with thunderstorms occurring frequently during the spring and summer.
These occasionally bring large hail and frequent lightning.

Particularly destructive ones have struck the Wichita area several times in the course of its history - in September 1965, during the ___E:Andover, Kansas tornado outbreak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andover_tornado_outbreak)___ of April 1991, and during the ___E:Oklahoma tornado outbreak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Oklahoma_tornado_outbreak)___ of May 1999.

Winters are cold and dry. Since Wichita is roughly midway between ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ and the ___E:Gulf of Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico)___ , cold spells and warm spells are equally frequent.
Warm air masses from the Gulf of Mexico can raise midwinter temperatures into the 50s and even 60s (°F).
Cold-air masses from the Arctic can occasionally plunge the temperature below 0 °F. Wind speed in the city averages 13 mph (21 km/h).
On average, January is the coldest month and the driest.
July is the hottest, and May the wettest.
The average temperature in Wichita is 57.7 °F (14.3 °C).

Over the course of a year, the monthly daily average temperature ranges from 33.2 °F (0.7 °C) in January to 81.5 °F (27.5 °C) in July. The high temperature reaches or exceeds 90 °F (32 °C) an average of 65 days a year, and 100 °F (38 °C) an average of 12 days a year. The minimum temperature falls to or below 10 °F (−12 °C) on an average 7.7 days a year.

The hottest temperature recorded in Wichita was 114 °F (46 °C) in 1936. The coldest temperature recorded was −22 °F (−30 °C) on ___E:February 12, 1899 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Blizzard_of_1899)___ .

Readings as low as −17 °F (−27 °C) and as high as 111 °F (44 °C) occurred as recently as February 16, 2021, and ___E:July 29–30, 2012 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_2012_North_American_heat_wave)___ , respectively.
Wichita receives on average about 34.31 inches (871 mm) of precipitation a year, most of which falls in the warmer months, and experiences 87 days of measurable precipitation.
The average ___E:relative humidity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_humidity)___ is 80% in the morning and 49% in the evening.
Annual snowfall averages 12.7 inches (32 cm).

Measurable snowfall occurs an average of nine days per year, with at least an inch of snow falling on four of those days. Snow depth of at least an inch occurs an average of 12 days per year.  The average window for freezing temperatures is October 25 to April 9.

Wichita is consistently ranked as one of the worst major cities in the nation for seasonal allergies, due largely to tree and grass pollen (partly from surrounding open plains and pastureland), and smoke from frequent burning of fields by the region's farmers and ranchers, driven by the strong Kansas winds.

The ___E:Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma_and_Allergy_Foundation_of_America)___ , ranked Wichita—out of the nation's 100 largest cities—sixth worst for people with allergies in 2016,  third worst in 2021,  second worst in 2022,  and worst nationwide in 2023.
Wichita has several recognized areas and neighborhoods.

The ___E:downtown area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Wichita)___ is generally considered to be east of the Arkansas River, west of Washington Street, north of Kellogg, and south of 13th Street.

It contains landmarks such as ___E:Century II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_II_Performing_Arts_%26_Convention_Center)___ , the ___E:Garvey Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/250_Douglas_Place)___ , and the ___E:Epic Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_Center)___ .

Old Town is also part of downtown; this 50-acre (0.20 km 2 ) area is home to a cluster of nightclubs, bars, restaurants, a movie theater, shops, and apartments and condominiums, many of which make use of historical warehouse-type spaces.

Two notable residential areas of Wichita are ___E:Riverside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside,_Wichita,_Kansas)___ and ___E:College Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Hill,_Wichita,_Kansas)___ .
Riverside is northwest of downtown, across the Arkansas River, and surrounds the 120-acre (0.49 km 2 ) Riverside Park.  College Hill is east of downtown and south of Wichita State University.

It is one of the more historic neighborhoods, along with ___E:Delano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delano,_Wichita,_Kansas)___ on the west side and ___E:Midtown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown,_Wichita,_Kansas)___ in the north-central city.

Four other historic neighborhoods—developed in southeast Wichita (particularly near ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ , ___E:Cessna U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_Aircraft)___ and ___E:Beech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beech_Aircraft)___ aircraft plants) -- are among the nation's few remaining examples of U.S. government-funded temporary ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ housing developments to support war factory personnel: Beechwood (now mostly demolished), Oaklawn, Hilltop (the city's highest-density large neighborhood), and massive Planeview (where over 30 languages are spoken) -- in all, home to about a fifth of the city's population at their peak. Though designed as temporary housing, all have remained occupied into the 21st century, most becoming low-income neighborhoods.

In terms of population, Wichita is the largest city in Kansas and the 49th largest city in the United States, according to the ___E:2020 census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census)___ .
Wichita has an extensive history of attracting immigrants.

Starting in 1895, a population of ___E:Lebanese Americans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_Americans)___ moved to the city, many of whom were ___E:Orthodox Christians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Christianity)___ .
A second wave of Lebanese migrants moved to Wichita to flee the ___E:Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_Civil_War)___ in their homeland.

Thousands of ___E:immigrants from Vietnam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_Americans)___ moved to Wichita in the aftermath of the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ .

Wichita is the principal city of both the Wichita ___E:Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Statistical_Area)___ and the Wichita-Winfield ___E:Combined Statistical Area (CSA) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_Statistical_Area)___ .

The Wichita MSA encompasses Sedgwick, ___E:Butler U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Kansas)___ , ___E:Harvey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_County,_Kansas)___ , and ___E:Sumner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumner_County,_Kansas)___ counties and, as of 2010, had a population of 623,061, making it the 84th largest MSA in the United States.

The larger Wichita-Winfield CSA also includes ___E:Cowley County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowley_County,_Kansas)___ and, as of 2013, had an estimated population of 673,598.  Nearby ___E:Reno County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reno_County)___ is not a part of the Wichita MSA or Wichita-Winfield CSA, but, were it included, it would add an additional population of 64,511 as of 2010.
Restaurants founded in Wichita include ___E:White Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Castle_(restaurant))___ and ___E:Pizza Hut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_Hut)___ .

A survey of well-known Kansas-based brands conducted by RSM Marketing Services and the Wichita Consumer Research Center showed many of the top-25 Kansas-based brands such as ___E:Koch, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koch,_Inc.)___ , ___E:Coleman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Company)___ , ___E:Cessna U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna)___ , Pizza Hut, ___E:Beechcraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechcraft)___ , ___E:Freddy's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddy%27s_Frozen_Custard_%26_Steakburgers)___ , and more are based in Wichita.

Wichita's principal ___E:industrial sector U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_sector)___ is ___E:manufacturing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing)___ , which accounted for 21.6% of area employment in 2003. Aircraft manufacturing has long dominated the local economy, and plays such an important role that it has the ability to influence the economic health of the entire region; the state offers tax breaks and other incentives to aircraft manufacturers.

___E:Healthcare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare)___ is Wichita's second-largest industry, employing about 28,000 people in the local area. Since healthcare needs remain fairly consistent regardless of the economy, this field was not subject to the same pressures that affected other industries in the early 2000s.
The Kansas Spine Hospital opened in 2004, as did a critical-care tower at ___E:Wesley Medical Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_Medical_Center)___ .
In July 2010, Via Christi Health, which is the largest provider of healthcare services in Kansas, opened a hospital that will serve the northwest area of Wichita.
Via Christi Hospital on St. Teresa is the system's fifth hospital to serve the Wichita community.
In 2016, Wesley Healthcare opened Wesley Children's Hospital, the first and only children's hospital in the Wichita area.

Thanks to the early 20th-century oil boom in neighboring ___E:Butler County, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Kansas)___ , Wichita became a major oil town, with dozens of oil-exploration companies and support enterprises.
Most famous of these was ___E:Koch, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koch,_Inc.)___ , today a global natural-resources conglomerate.

The city was also at one time the headquarters of the former ___E:Derby Oil Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_Oil_Company)___ , which was purchased by ___E:Coastal Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_Corporation)___ in 1988.

___E:Koch, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koch,_Inc.)___ and ___E:Cargill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargill)___ , the two largest privately held companies in the United States, both operate headquarters facilities in Wichita.

The ___E:Koch, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koch,_Inc.)___ global corporate headquarters is in a large office-tower complex in northeast Wichita. ___E:Cargill Meat Solutions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargill_Meat_Solutions)___ , at one time the nation's third-largest beef producer, is headquartered downtown.

Other firms with headquarters in Wichita include amusement ride manufacturer ___E:Chance Rides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chance_Rides)___ , gourmet food retailer ___E:Dean & Deluca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_%26_Deluca)___ , ___E:renewable energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy)___ company Alternative Energy Solutions, and ___E:Coleman Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Company)___ , a manufacturer of camping and outdoor recreation supplies. ___E:Air Midwest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Midwest)___ , the first officially certificated "commuter" airline in the U.S., was founded and headquartered in Wichita and evolved into the nation's eighth-largest regional airline prior to its dissolution in 2008.
As of 2013, 68.2% of the population over the age of 16 was in the labor force; 0.6% was in the armed forces, and 67.6% was in the civilian labor force with 61.2% employed and 6.4% unemployed.

The occupational composition of the employed civilian labor force was 33.3% in management, business, science, and arts; 25.1% in sales and office occupations; 17.2% in service occupations; 14.0% in production, transportation, and material moving; and 10.4% in natural resources, construction, and maintenance.

The three industries employing the largest percentages of the working civilian labor force were educational services, health care, and social assistance (22.3%); manufacturing (19.2%); and retail trade (11.0%).

The cost of living in Wichita is below average; compared to a U.S. average of 100, the cost of living index for the city is 84.0.  As of 2013, the median home value in the city was $117,500, the median selected monthly owner cost was $1,194 for housing units with a mortgage and $419 for those without, and the median gross rent was $690.

From the early to late 20th century, aircraft pioneers such as Clyde Cessna, Emil Matthew "Matty" Laird, Lloyd Stearman, ___E:Walter Beech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Beech)___ , ___E:Al Mooney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Mooney)___ and ___E:Bill Lear U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Lear)___ began aircraft-manufacturing enterprises that led to Wichita becoming the nation's leading city in numbers of aircraft produced, earning Wichita, in 1928, the 1929 title "Air Capital City" from the nation's ___E:Aeronautical Chamber of Commerce U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Industries_Association)___ — a title the city would claim permanently.

The aircraft corporations ___E:E. M. Laird Aviation Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swallow_Airplane_Company)___ (the nation's first successful commercial airplane manufacturer), ___E:Travel Air U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_Air)___ (started by Beech, Stearman, and Cessna), ___E:Stearman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stearman_Aircraft)___ , ___E:Cessna U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna)___ , ___E:Beechcraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechcraft)___ , and ___E:Mooney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mooney_Airplane_Company)___ were all founded in Wichita between 1920 and early 1932.     By 1931, ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ (of ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ , Washington) had absorbed Stearman, creating "Boeing-Wichita", which would eventually grow to become Kansas' largest employer.
During ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , employment peak at Boeing-Wichita was 29,795 in December 1943.

Today, Cessna Aircraft Co. (the world's highest-volume airplane manufacturer) and Beechcraft remain based in Wichita, having merged into ___E:Textron Aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textron_Aviation)___ in 2014, along with ___E:Learjet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learjet)___ and Boeing's chief sub-assembly supplier, ___E:Spirit AeroSystems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_AeroSystems)___ .

Airbus maintains a workforce in Wichita, and ___E:Bombardier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_Aerospace)___ (parent company of Learjet) has other divisions in Wichita, as well. Over 50 other aviation businesses operate in the Wichita MSA, as well as over 350 suppliers and subcontractors to the local aircraft manufacturers.
In total, Wichita and its companies have manufactured an estimated 250,000 aircraft since Clyde Cessna's first Wichita-built aircraft in 1916.

In the early 2000s, a national and international recession combined with the after-effects of the ___E:September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ to depress the aviation subsector in and around Wichita.

Orders for new aircraft plummeted, prompting Wichita's five largest aircraft manufacturers, Boeing Co., Cessna Aircraft Co., Bombardier Learjet Inc., ___E:Hawker Beechcraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Beechcraft)___ , and ___E:Raytheon Aircraft Co. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon)___ —to slash a combined 15,000 jobs between 2001 and 2004. In response, these companies began developing small- and mid-sized airplanes to appeal to business and corporate users.

In 2007, Wichita built 977 aircraft, ranging from single-engine ___E:light aircraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_aircraft)___ to the world's fastest civilian jet; one-fifth of the civilian aircraft produced in United States that year, plus numerous small military aircraft.

In early 2012, Boeing announced it would be closing its Wichita plant by the end of 2013,   which paved the road for ___E:Spirit Aerosystems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_AeroSystems)___ to open its plant (actually, the Boeing-Wichita factory, still producing the same aircraft assemblies for Boeing, but officially under a different corporation).
Wichita is home to several art museums and performing arts groups.
The ___E:Wichita Art Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Art_Museum)___ is the largest art museum in the state of Kansas and contains 7,000 works in permanent collections.

The Ulrich Museum of Art at ___E:Wichita State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_State_University)___ is a modern and contemporary art museum with over 6,300 works in its permanent collection.

Wichita is the music hub of central Kansas, and draws major acts from around the world, performing at various concert halls, arenas, and stadiums around the area. Most major rock'n'roll and pop-music stars, and virtually all country music stars, perform there during their career. [citation needed]

___E:Music Theatre Wichita U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Theatre_Wichita)___ , Wichita Grand Opera (both nationally renowned),  and the ___E:Wichita Symphony Orchestra U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Symphony_Orchestra)___ perform regularly at the ___E:Century II Convention Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_II_Convention_Hall)___ downtown.
Concerts are also regularly performed by the nationally noted schools of music at Wichita's two largest universities.

The ___E:Orpheum Theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheum_Theatre_(Wichita))___ , a classic ___E:movie palace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_palace)___ built in 1922, serves as a downtown venue for smaller shows.
The ___E:Cotillion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotillion_Ballroom)___ , a special events facility built in 1960, serves a similar purpose as a music venue.

The ___E:Wichita River Festival U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wichita_River_Festival&action=edit&redlink=1)___ has been held in the Downtown and Old Town areas of the city since 1972. It has featured events, musical entertainment, sporting events, traveling exhibits, cultural and historical activities, ___E:plays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theatre))___ , interactive children's events, a ___E:flea market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flea_market)___ , river events, a ___E:parade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade)___ , ___E:block parties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_parties)___ , a food court, ___E:fireworks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks)___ , and ___E:souvenirs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souvenir)___ for the roughly 370,000+ patrons who attend each year.  In 2011, the festival was moved from May to June because of rain during previous festivals.
The Wichita River Festival has seen immense growth, with record numbers in 2016 and again in 2018.  Much of that growth is attributed to attractive musical acts at the festival.

Wichita customarily holds major parades for the River Festival, ___E:Christmas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas)___ season (shortly after ___E:Thanksgiving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving_(United_States))___ ), ___E:Veterans Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_Day)___ , ___E:Juneteenth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneteenth)___ , and ___E:St. Patrick's Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Patrick%27s_Day)___ .
The annual Wichita Black Arts Festival, held in the spring, celebrates the arts, crafts, and creativity of Wichita's large African-American community.
It usually takes place in Central-Northeast Wichita.
A ___E:Juneteenth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneteenth)___ event and parade also are common annual events.

The annual Wichita Asian Festival, usually held at Century II in October, displays the native arts, crafts, cultural performances and foods of Wichita's large, diverse Asian community from the Middle East, Central and South Asia, Southeast Asia and East Asia. The event includes many varied performances of Asian music, dance, acrobatics and martial arts, talent pageant, and vendors of Asian arts and crafts.
Dozens of food vendors serve the cuisine of most Asian nations.

The International Student Association at ___E:Wichita State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_State_University)___ presents an annual international cultural exhibition and food festival, on the campus at WSU, providing an inexpensive sampling of global culture and cuisine to the general public.

One or more large ___E:Renaissance fairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_fair)___ occur annually, including the "RenFair" in conjunction with the "Kingdom of Calontir" of the SCA ( ___E:Society for Creative Anachronism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Creative_Anachronism)___ ).
The fairs vary in length from one day to a week, typically at Sedgwick County Park or ___E:Newman University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newman_University_(Kansas))___ .

The ___E:Wichita Public Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Public_Library)___ 's Academy Awards Shorts program is reportedly the oldest annual, complete, free public screening outside of Hollywood of the full array of ___E:short films U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film)___ nominated for an ___E:Academy Award ("Oscar") U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards)___ .

In late winter, shortly before the Academy Awards ceremonies, the films—including all nominated documentary, live action, and animated shorts—are presented, free, at the Library and in local theaters and other venues around Wichita.

Wichita's former Congressman, ___E:Motion Picture Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association)___ President ___E:Dan Glickman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Glickman)___ , has served as honorary chair of the event, and some of the filmmakers have attended and visited with the audiences.

The ___E:Tallgrass Film Festival U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallgrass_Film_Festival)___ has been held in downtown Wichita since 2003. It draws over 100 independent feature and short films from all over the world for three days each October.
Notable people from the entertainment industry have attended the festival.

Aviation-related events are common in the Wichita area, including ___E:air shows U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_show)___ , ___E:fly-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly-in)___ , air races, aviation conferences, exhibitions, and trade shows.

The city's two main air shows, which are generally held in alternating years, are the city-sponsored civilian Wichita Flight Festival  (originally the "Kansas Flight Festival") and the military-sponsored McConnell Air Force Base Open House and Airshow.

A wide range of car shows are also common in Wichita,     including the Blacktop Nationals,    the Automobilia show (claiming over 1,000 vehicles on display  ),  and the Riverfest Classic Car Show,  each of which fill much of downtown Wichita.
Wichita is also home to the large Cars for Charities Rod & Custom Car Show (started in 1957 as the Darryl Starbird Show), one of the longest-running indoor car shows in the nation.

Museums and landmarks devoted to science, culture, and area history are located throughout the city. Several lie along the ___E:Arkansas River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_River)___ west of downtown, including the ___E:Exploration Place U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploration_Place)___ science and discovery center, the ___E:Mid-America All-Indian Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-America_All-Indian_Center)___ , the ___E:Old Cowtown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Cowtown_Museum)___ living history museum, and ___E:The Keeper of the Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Keeper_of_the_Plains)___ statue and its associated display highlighting the daily lives of ___E:Plains Indians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plains_Indians)___ .

The ___E:Wichita-Sedgwick County Historical Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita-Sedgwick_County_Historical_Museum)___ in downtown Wichita occupies the original Wichita city hall, built in 1892. The museum contains artifacts that tell the story of Wichita and Sedgwick County starting from 1865 and continuing to the present day.  Nearby is the 1913 ___E:Sedgwick County Memorial Hall and Soldiers and Sailors Monument U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedgwick_County_Memorial_Hall_and_Soldiers_and_Sailors_Monument)___ .

East of downtown is the ___E:Museum of World Treasures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_World_Treasures)___ and railroad-oriented ___E:Great Plains Transportation Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plains_Transportation_Museum)___ .

The Coleman Factory Outlet and Museum was at 235 N St. Francis street and was the home of the ___E:Coleman Lantern U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Lantern)___ until it closed in 2018. Wichita suffered severe floods of the Arkansas river in 1877, 1904, 1916, 1923, 1944, 1951 and 1955. In 1944 the city flooded 3 times in 11 days. The project was completed in 1958. The Big Ditch diverts part of the Arkansas River's flow around west-central Wichita, running roughly parallel to the ___E:Interstate 235 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_235_(Kansas))___ bypass.

A second flood control canal lies between the lanes of ___E:Interstate 135 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_135)___ , running south through the central part of the city. Chisholm Creek is diverted into this canal for most of its length.
The city's flood defenses were tested in the ___E:Great Flood of 1993 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1993)___ .
Flooding that year kept the Big Ditch full for more than a month and caused $6 million of damage to the flood control infrastructure.

The damage was not fully repaired until 2007.  In 2019, the Floodway was renamed the ___E:MS Mitch Mitchell Floodway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MS_Mitch_Mitchell_Floodway)___ in honor of the man credited for its creation.

Both its northern and southern termini are interchanges with I-135. ___E:U.S. Routes 54 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_54_in_Kansas)___ and ___E:400 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_400)___ run concurrently through Wichita as Kellogg Avenue, the city's primary east-west artery, with interchanges, from west to east, with I-235, I-135, and I-35. ___E:U.S. Route 81 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_81_in_Kansas)___ , a north–south route, enters Wichita from the south as Broadway, turns east as 47th Street South for approximately half a mile, and then runs concurrently north with I-135 through the rest of the city. ___E:K-96 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-96_(Kansas_highway))___ , an east–west route, enters the city from the northwest, runs concurrently with I-235 through north-central Wichita, turns south for approximately a mile, running concurrently with I-135 before splitting off to the east and traveling around northeastern Wichita, ultimately terminating at an interchange with U.S. 54/U.S. 400 in the eastern part of the city. ___E:K-254 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-254_(Kansas_highway))___ begins at I-235's interchange with I-135 in north-central Wichita and exits the city to the northeast. ___E:K-15 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-15_(Kansas_highway))___ , a north–south route, enters the city from the south and joins I-135 and U.S. 81 in south-central Wichita, running concurrently with them through the rest of the city. ___E:K-42 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-42_(Kansas_highway))___ enters the city from the southwest and terminates at its interchange with U.S. 54/U.S. 400 in west-central Wichita.

___E:Wichita Transit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Transit)___ operates 53 buses on 18 fixed bus routes within the city. The organization reports over 2 million trips per year (5,400 trips per day) on its fixed routes.
Wichita Transit also operates a demand response ___E:paratransit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paratransit)___ service with 320,800 passenger trips annually.
A 2005 study ranked Wichita near the bottom of the fifty largest American cities in terms of percentage of commuters using public transit.
Only 0.5% used it to get to or from work.

The Wichita Airport Authority manages the city's two main public airports, ___E:Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Dwight_D._Eisenhower_National_Airport)___ and ___E:Colonel James Jabara Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_James_Jabara_Airport)___ .
Located in the western part of the city, Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport is the city's primary airport as well as the largest airport in Kansas.

Seven commercial airlines (Alaska, Allegiant, American, Delta, Frontier, Southwest & United) serve Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport with non-stop flights to several U.S. ___E:airline hubs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airline_hub)___ .

Jabara Airport is a ___E:general aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation)___ facility on the city's northeast side.  The city also has several privately owned airports. ___E:Cessna Aircraft Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_Aircraft_Field)___ and ___E:Beech Factory Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beech_Factory_Airport)___ , operated by manufacturers Cessna and Beechcraft, respectively, lie in east Wichita.
Two smaller airports, Riverside Airport and Westport Airport, are in west Wichita.
The first train arrived in Wichita on May 16, 1872 from Newton with 44 passengers.
Numerous passenger depots served the city up until 1979, with two depots remaining extant.

Two ___E:Class I railroads U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_I_railroad)___ , ___E:BNSF Railway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BNSF_Railway)___ and ___E:Union Pacific Railroad (UP) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad)___ , operate freight rail lines through Wichita.

UP's OKT Line runs generally north-south through the city; north of downtown, the line consists of trackage leased to BNSF.   An additional UP line enters the city from the northeast and terminates downtown.

BNSF's main line through the city enters from the north, passes through downtown, and exits to the southeast, paralleling highway K-15.   The ___E:Wichita Terminal Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Terminal_Association)___ , a joint operation between BNSF and UP, provides ___E:switching U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switching_(railroad))___ service on three miles (5 km) of track downtown.

In addition, two lines of the ___E:Kansas and Oklahoma Railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_and_Oklahoma_Railroad)___ enter the city, one from the northwest and the other from the southwest, both terminating at their junction in west-central Wichita.

Wichita has not had passenger rail service since 1979.  The nearest ___E:Amtrak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak)___ station is in ___E:Newton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Kansas)___ 25 miles (40 km) north, offering service on the Southwest Chief line between ___E:Los Angeles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California)___ and ___E:Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago)___ .

Amtrak offers bus service from downtown Wichita to its ___E:station in Newton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_station_(Kansas))___ as well as to its ___E:station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_Depot_(Oklahoma_City))___ in ___E:Oklahoma City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City)___ , the northern terminus of the Heartland Flyer line.
A 2014 study by ___E:Walk Score U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk_Score)___ ranked Wichita 41st most walkable of fifty largest U.S. cities.

After numerous citizen surveys showed Wichitans want better bicycle infrastructure, The Wichita Bicycle Master Plan, a set of guidelines toward the development of a 149-mile Priority Bicycle Network, was endorsed by the Wichita City Council on February 5, 2013, as a guide to future infrastructure planning and development.
As a result, Wichita's bikeways covered 115 miles of the city by 2018. One-third of the bikeways were added between 2011, when the plan was still in development, and 2018.
